audience: HTTP/API engineers learning interview-sized DNS reasoning. Any .example names in assessment scenarios are illustrative, not public deployments.
prerequisites: An HTTP client sends a request with a method, path, headers and optional body to a server and receives a response with a status and optional body. HTTPS encrypts HTTP in transit.
An API server can read and write a database; the database stores application data.

objectives.description: Define DNS as name discovery and distinguish resolving the hostname from the later HTTPS request and its path. Define a hostname, IP address, DNS record and cache; explain that an address identifies a network destination and does not prove the destination service is healthy.

Define a stub resolver, recursive resolver, authoritative server, zone and delegation. Trace a simplified address lookup with empty relevant caches through root, top-level-domain and domain authorities, distinguishing referrals from the final authoritative answer and noting cache reuse can skip these visits.

Distinguish A as an IPv4 address record, AAAA as an IPv6 address record, and CNAME as a name alias. Define IPv4/IPv6 as address families. Trace a hostname aliasing another hostname and the target address lookup; explain why the alias alone supplies no IP address and adds target DNS dependencies.

Define TTL as the time-to-live limiting ordinary cache reuse of a DNS record, not a global update timer. Plan an address change by reducing TTL early enough for previous longer-lived cache entries to age out, allowing overlap and monitoring both destinations; explain query/availability costs of shorter TTLs and why independent caches and connection lifetimes prevent a guaranteed worldwide cutover instant.

Define negative caching and distinguish NXDOMAIN (name does not exist), NODATA (name exists but requested record type is absent), and resolution failure such as SERVFAIL. Explain delayed discovery after adding a name or record, using the negative answer's own cache lifetime rather than a newly added positive TTL; failures may also be cached and are not proof of name absence.

Define DNS traffic steering and failover as selecting returned destinations and changing them after failure. Explain that health detection and policy changes are separate mechanisms; cached answers, shared resolvers and existing connections limit per-request control, exact traffic splits and failover speed. Require reachable healthy capacity at the replacement.

Distinguish DNS availability from application availability. Explain why existing cached answers or connections can work while fresh lookups fail; identify recursive-resolver and authoritative/delegation dependencies, and limits of redundant DNS servers. Diagnose name resolution before connection/HTTPS and HTTP service errors without treating successful DNS as proof of application health.

Define DNSSEC as validation of signed DNS data through a chain of trust and distinguish it from HTTPS certificate-based endpoint authentication and transport encryption. Explain that DNSSEC does not encrypt queries or attest service health, and that clients must still verify HTTPS identity for the requested hostname even after valid DNS resolution.

questions.question: A new client requests https://api.notes.example/notes/42 with empty relevant caches. In a teaching hierarchy, root delegates .example, .example delegates notes.example, and api.notes.example aliases edge.notes.example, which has A and AAAA records. Trace the stub, recursive resolver, referrals and authoritative answer; define their roles, delegation and zone. Explain A, AAAA and CNAME, the target-address dependency and later cache reuse. Identify the part DNS resolves and the later connection/HTTPS path, and explain whether an address proves Notes is healthy.
criteria: DNS resolves api.notes.example to address information before a connection can be established when no usable address is already available; HTTPS then carries the request to /notes/42.
DNS does not route by the HTTP path or carry the subsequent HTTP exchange, and an address answer does not establish service health.
The stub is the client-side lookup helper; the recursive resolver obtains the answer on the client's behalf; an authoritative server answers for a zone, a managed portion of DNS names.

Delegation assigns responsibility for a child zone and a referral points toward its authoritative servers; the recursive resolver follows root and .example referrals to the notes.example authority for the final record.
The stub asks the recursive resolver rather than independently requiring every authority visit; usable cached answers or delegations can shorten or eliminate those visits.
IPv4 and IPv6 are IP address families; A supplies an IPv4 address and AAAA an IPv6 address.
CNAME points to another DNS name, not a URL, HTTP path or IP address; resolution follows the alias and obtains target address records, possibly from caches.
The alias alone does not supply a connectable address; reaching the target's address data is an additional DNS dependency, and alias and target records can be cached separately.
criticalMisconceptions: DNS servers carry every subsequent HTTP request or route /notes/42.
Root stores every final address.
A CNAME supplies an IP address without target resolution.

questions.question: api.notes.example had a 3600-second TTL. At noon you lower it to 60 seconds and change its address. A resolver cached the old answer at 11:59. Explain TTL and whether that resolver must refresh by 12:01. Describe a safer planned change, including when to lower TTL, how long to keep the old destination usable and what to monitor. Explain the query/dependency cost of short TTLs and why TTL is not a worldwide cutover guarantee.
criteria: TTL limits ordinary reuse of a cached record; lowering the authoritative TTL does not rewrite existing cache entries, so the 11:59 answer can remain ordinarily usable until about 12:59.

Reduce TTL ahead of the change and allow the prior longer TTL to age out before switching; keep the old destination usable during the transition and monitor traffic/errors at both destinations, including existing connections.
Shorter TTLs usually require more DNS refreshes and more frequent dependence on working resolution; separate caches and existing connections prevent a guaranteed simultaneous global cutover.
criticalMisconceptions: A lower TTL immediately updates every cache.
All clients switch destinations exactly one new TTL after an edit.
A shorter TTL has no cost.

questions.question: Before deployment a resolver cached NXDOMAIN for api.notes.example. You add the name with a 30-second A-record TTL, but that resolver still reports absence. Define negative caching and explain why the new positive TTL does not necessarily clear the result. Contrast NXDOMAIN, a response with no AAAA record for an existing name (NODATA), and SERVFAIL, including whether a failure may be cached and what each result does or does not prove.
criteria: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence; an already cached negative answer follows its own cache lifetime and is not overwritten merely by adding a positive record or setting its TTL to 30 seconds.
NXDOMAIN reports that the queried name does not exist; NODATA reports no record of the queried type for an existing name and does not imply no A record or no name.
SERVFAIL indicates resolution could not be completed, not authoritative proof of name absence; resolution failures may also be cached.
criticalMisconceptions: A newly added record's TTL immediately clears old NXDOMAIN answers.
No AAAA record means the name does not exist.
SERVFAIL proves NXDOMAIN or can never be cached.

questions.question: Notes has east and west endpoints. A DNS policy returns each for some lookups; east fails and you want to send everyone west. Define steering and failover, explain how health detection and answer changes must occur, why equal DNS answers do not ensure half of HTTP requests reach each endpoint, and why removing east does not instantly move cached clients or existing connections. State what west needs for successful recovery.
criteria: DNS steering selects destinations in answers; failover changes the selected destination after failure, requiring a separate health signal and policy or operator that changes answers.
DNS answers are reused by clients and shared recursive resolvers; lookup proportions do not equal HTTP-request proportions and DNS cannot choose anew for every request on an existing connection.
Old cached answers can still select east and existing connections do not migrate merely because DNS changed; DNS change alone supplies no instant recovery guarantee.
West must be reachable, healthy and have enough capacity to serve redirected load; DNS cannot create that capacity or make the service healthy.
criticalMisconceptions: DNS automatically detects application failures.
A 50/50 DNS policy guarantees a 50/50 HTTP-request split.
Removing an address instantly migrates existing connections.

questions.question: Some Notes users with open sessions still work while new users cannot resolve api.notes.example. Another user resolves the expected address but receives an HTTP 500. Explain how cache/connection reuse permits these different outcomes. Describe how to separate a resolver or authoritative/delegation problem from a connection/HTTPS or application problem, and what redundant DNS servers help with versus shared bad records or a failed Notes service.
criteria: Cached addresses can avoid a fresh lookup and open connections can continue without a DNS query; fresh uncached lookups still depend on functioning resolution.

Check the queried name/type and answer or error at the client's recursive resolver; compare authoritative data/delegation when resolution is wrong or failing, distinguishing missing data from resolution failure.

Once the expected address is obtained, inspect connection/HTTPS and application results separately; an HTTP 500 means an HTTP service responded with an error and is not by itself a DNS lookup failure.
Reachable alternate resolvers or authoritative servers can reduce individual DNS-server failures but cannot fix shared incorrect records/delegation or restore a failed Notes service.
criticalMisconceptions: A DNS outage immediately stops all existing sessions.
DNS success proves the service is healthy.
More DNS servers repair shared wrong records.

questions.question: A validating resolver reports a DNSSEC-validated answer for api.notes.example. Define DNSSEC and its chain of trust and state what successful validation establishes. Does it hide the query, prove Notes is healthy, or remove the need to check the HTTPS certificate? Explain what HTTPS authenticates and encrypts and which hostname the client must verify.
criteria: DNSSEC uses signatures linked through a chain of trust to validate DNS data origin and integrity; successful validation does not certify the application behind the returned address.
DNSSEC does not encrypt DNS queries or prove service health.
HTTPS checks the endpoint certificate against the requested hostname api.notes.example and encrypts HTTP transport; DNSSEC does not replace those checks.
criticalMisconceptions: DNSSEC encrypts DNS traffic.
A DNSSEC-validated address makes HTTPS certificate verification unnecessary.
DNSSEC proves the application is trustworthy or healthy.

questions.question: A client wants https://api.notes.example/notes/42. Define hostname, IP address, DNS record and cache. criticalMisconceptions: Every HTTP request passes through DNS servers.
DNS selects a backend based on /notes/42.
A DNS answer proves the application is available.
